title: Minimum wage increase on restaurant employment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Difference-in-differences (DID) is the appropriate method here. We compare the change in employment before/after the minimum wage increase in treated states versus the change in control states. The key assumption is parallel trends: treated and control restaurants would have followed similar employment trajectories absent the minimum wage increase.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(fixest)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s02_data.csv")

# Basic data summary
cat("Data Summary:\n")
cat("Total observations:", nrow(data), "\n")
cat("Unique restaurants:", length(unique(data$unit_id)), "\n")
cat("Time periods:", min(data$period), "to", max(data$period), "\n")
cat("Treated units:", sum(data$treated == 1 & data$period == 1), "\n")
cat("Control units:", sum(data$treated == 0 & data$period == 1), "\n")

# Main DID regression with restaurant and time fixed effects
did_model <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, data = data)

cat("\n=== MAIN DID RESULTS ===\n")
print(summary(did_model))

# Extract and print the key coefficient
did_coef <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
did_se <- se(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
cat("\nDID Coefficient (Treatment Effect):", round(did_coef, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(did_se, 4), "\n")
cat("95% CI: [", round(did_coef - 1.96*did_se, 4), ",", round(did_coef + 1.96*did_se, 4), "]\n")

# Convert to percentage change (since y is in logs)
pct_change <- (exp(did_coef) - 1) * 100
cat("Percentage change in employment:", round(pct_change, 2), "%\n")

# Robustness check 1: Pre-trend test
# Test if treated and control groups had parallel trends before treatment
pre_data <- data[data$period < 4, ]
pre_trend_model <- feols(y ~ treated:factor(period) | unit_id + period, data = pre_data)

cat("\n=== PRE-TREND TEST ===\n")
print(summary(pre_trend_model))

# Robustness check 2: Event study specification
# Create relative time variables
data$rel_time <- data$period - 4
data$rel_time[data$treated == 0] <- 0

# Event study regression (excluding period -1 as base)
event_model <- feols(y ~ i(rel_time, treated, ref = -1) | unit_id + period, 
                     data = data)

cat("\n=== EVENT STUDY RESULTS ===\n")
print(summary(event_model))

# Robustness check 3: Alternative specification without unit FE
simple_did <- feols(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post | period, data = data)

cat("\n=== ROBUSTNESS: WITHOUT UNIT FE ===\n")
cat("DID Coefficient:", round(coef(simple_did)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(se(simple_did)["treat_x_post"], 4), "\n")

# Final summary
cat("\n=== SUMMARY ===\n")
cat("Main finding: Minimum wage increase", 
    ifelse(did_coef < 0, "reduced", "increased"), 
    "restaurant employment by", round(abs(pct_change), 2), "%\n")
cat("Statistical significance:", 
    ifelse(abs(did_coef/did_se) > 1.96, "Significant at 5% level", "Not significant at 5% level"), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect a negative coefficient around -0.05 to -0.15 (corresponding to a 5-15% reduction in employment). Economic theory suggests that minimum wage increases raise labor costs, potentially leading restaurants to reduce employment, especially for entry-level positions common in fast food. However, the magnitude depends on demand elasticity and restaurants' ability to pass costs to consumers through higher prices.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=high-wage states, control=neighboring states; shock=minimum wage hike
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Modest employment decline in treated restaurants post minimum wage increase
